nodes.name: Decidability of the first-order theory of (R^2, betweenness, equidistance)
nodes.statement: Tarski established in \cite{Tarski:1948} that the first-order theory of $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta,\equiv)$ is decidable.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: the first-order theory of $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta,\equiv)$ is decidable

nodes.name: Aiello-van Benthem conjecture
nodes.statement: In \cite{vanBenthemAiello:2002}, Aiello and van Benthem pose the question: ``\emph{What is the complete monadic $\Pi^1_1$ theory of the affine real plane}?'' By \emph{affine real plane}, the authors refer to the structure $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta)$. The monadic $\Pi_1^1$-theory of $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta)$ is of course essentially the same as the first-order theory of the class of expansions $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta,(P_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}})$ of the the affine real plane $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta)$ by unary predicates $P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$. Aiello and van Benthem conjecture that the theory is decidable.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The monadic Pi^1_1 theory of the affine real plane (R^2, beta) is conjectured decidable.
conclusions: Aiello and van Benthem conjecture that the theory is decidable.

nodes.name: Natural structures with undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement: Our results establish undecidability for a wide range of unary expansion classes of natural geometric structures $(T,\beta)$. In addition to $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta)$, such structures include for example the rational plane $(\mathbb{Q}^2,\beta)$, the real unit cube $([0,1]^3,\beta)$, and the plane of algebraic reals $(\mathbb{A}^2,\beta)$ --- to name a few.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Examples: (R^2,beta), (Q^2,beta), ([0,1]^3,beta), (A^2,beta).

nodes.name: Purely relational vocabulary
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ be a \emph{purely relational vocabulary}, i.e., a vocabulary that does not contain function symbols or constant symbols.
nodes.section: 2.1 Interpretations
differentia: does not contain function symbols or constant symbols

nodes.name: Uniform first-order interpretability
nodes.statement: Let $\tau$ be a vocabulary that does not contain function symbols. Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a nonempty class of $\sigma$-structures and $\mathcal{C}$ a nonempty class of $\tau$-structures. Assume that there exists a surjective map $F$ from $\mathcal{C}$ onto $\mathcal{B}$ and a first-order $\tau$-formula $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(x)$ in one free variable, $x$, such that for each structure $\mathfrak{C}\in\mathcal{C}$, there is a bijection $f$ from the domain of $F(\mathfrak{C})$ to the set $$\{\ u\in \mathit{Dom}(\mathfrak{C})\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\ \}.$$ Assume, furthermore, that for each relation symbol $R\in\sigma$, there is a first-order $\tau$-formula $\varphi_R(x_1,...,x_{\mathit{Ar}(R)})$ such that we have $$R^{F(\mathfrak{C})}(u_1,...,u_{\mathit{Ar}(R)})\ \Leftrightarrow\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_R\bigl(f(u_1),...,f(u_{\mathit{Ar}(R)})\bigr)$$ for every tuple $(u_1,...,u_{\mathit{Ar}(R)})\in(\mathit{Dom}(F(\mathfrak{C})))^{\mathit{Ar}(R)}$. Here $\mathit{Ar}(R)$ is the arity of $R$. We then say that the class $\mathcal{B}$ is \emph{uniformly first-order interpretable in $\mathcal{C}$}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Interpretations
nodes.statement_short: B is uniformly FO interpretable in C if FO formulas define, uniformly over C, a copy of each structure of B via a surjection F.

nodes.name: Uniform interpretation
nodes.statement: Assume that a class of $\sigma$-structures $\mathcal{B}$ is uniformly first-order interpretable in a class $\mathcal{C}$ of $\tau$-structures. Define a map $I$ from the set of first-order $\sigma$-formulae to the set of first-order $\tau$-formulae as follows. \begin{enumerate} \item If $k\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}$ and $R\in\sigma$ is a $k$-ary relation symbol, then $$I(R(x_1,...,x_k))\, :=\, \varphi_{R}(x_1,...,x_k),$$ where $\varphi_{R}(x_1,...,x_k)$ is a first-order formula for $R$ witnessing the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is uniformly first-order interpretable in\, $\mathcal{C}$. \item $I(x=y)\, :=\, x=y$. \item $I(\neg\varphi):=\neg I(\varphi)$. \item $I(\varphi\wedge\psi)\, :=\, I(\varphi)\wedge I(\psi)$. \item $I\bigl(\exists x\, \psi(x)\bigr)\, :=\, \exists x\bigl(\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(x)\wedge I(\psi(x))\bigr).$ \end{enumerate} We call the map $I$ a \emph{uniform interpretation of\, $\mathcal{B}$ in $\mathcal{C}$.}
nodes.section: 2.1 Interpretations
nodes.statement_short: The formula translation I replacing relation symbols by their defining formulas and relativising quantifiers to phi_Dom.

nodes.name: Uniform interpretation of a class of reducts
nodes.statement: Also, if $\mathcal{A}$ is the class of reducts of structures $\mathfrak{B}\in\mathcal{B}$ to some vocabulary $\rho\subseteq\sigma$, the function $I$ is called a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{A}$ in $\mathcal{C}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Interpretations

nodes.name: Uniform interpretation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\rho$ be a purely relational vocabulary and $\tau$ a vocabulary not containing function symbols. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a class of $\rho$-structure and\, $\mathcal{C}$ a class of $\tau$-structures. Let $I$ be a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{A}$ in $\mathcal{C}$. Let $\varphi$ be a first-order formula of the vocabulary $\rho$. Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a structure $\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}\models \varphi$. \item There exists a structure $\mathfrak{C}\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models I(\varphi)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1 Interpretations
assumptions: $\rho$ be a purely relational vocabulary and $\tau$ a vocabulary not containing function symbols
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a class of $\rho$-structure and\, $\mathcal{C}$ a class of $\tau$-structures.
Let $I$ be a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{A}$ in $\mathcal{C}$.
Let $\varphi$ be a first-order formula of the vocabulary $\rho$.
conclusions: the following conditions are equivalent.
equivalent_conditions: There exists a structure $\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{A}\models \varphi$.
There exists a structure $\mathfrak{C}\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models I(\varphi)$.
nodes.statement_short: phi is satisfiable in A iff its translation I(phi) is satisfiable in C.

nodes.statement: Straightforward.

nodes.name: Monadic second-order logic (MSO)
nodes.statement: \emph{Monadic second-order logic}, $\mathrm{MSO}$, extends first-order logic with quantification of relation symbols ranging over subsets of the domain of a model.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures
differentia: quantification of relation symbols ranging over subsets of the domain of a model

nodes.name: Universal and existential MSO
nodes.statement: In \emph{universal (existential) monadic second-order logic}, $\forall \mathrm{MSO}$ ($\exists \mathrm{MSO}$), the quantification of monadic relations is restricted to universal (existential) prenex quantification in the beginning of formulae.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Monadic Pi^1_1 and Sigma^1_1
nodes.statement: The logics $\forall \mathrm{MSO}$ and $\exists \mathrm{MSO}$ are also known as monadic $\Pi_1^1$ and monadic $\Sigma_1^1$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Weak monadic second-order logic (WMSO)
nodes.statement: \emph{Weak monadic second-order logic}, $\mathrm{WMSO}$, is a semantic variant of monadic second-order logic in which the quantified relation symbols range over finite subsets of the domain of a model.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures
nodes.genus: semantic variant of monadic second-order logic
differentia: the quantified relation symbols range over finite subsets of the domain of a model

nodes.name: Universal and existential WMSO
nodes.statement: The weak variants $\forall \mathrm{WMSO}$ and $\exists \mathrm{WMSO}$ of $\forall \mathrm{MSO}$ and $\exists\mathrm{MSO}$ are defined in the obvious way.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: MSO Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse game
nodes.statement: An $\mathrm{MSO}$ game is played by two players, the \emph{spoiler} and the \emph{duplicator}, on two structures $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ of the same purely relational vocabulary $\sigma$. A round starts by spoiler picking a structure, $\mathfrak{A}$ or $\mathfrak{B}$, and an element or a subset of that structure. The duplicator responds by choosing an object of the same type from the other structure. Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be the elements and $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ the subsets chosen in a $k$-round game from the structures $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$, respectively. Then the duplicator wins the game iff $(\vec{a},\vec{b})$ defines a partial isomorphism from $(\mathfrak{A},\vec{A})$ to $(\mathfrak{B},\vec{B})$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures
nodes.statement_short: Spoiler picks elements or subsets in one structure, duplicator answers in the other; duplicator wins if the choices give a partial isomorphism.

nodes.name: MSO Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse theorem
nodes.statement: The $k$-round game characterizes $\mathrm{MSO}[k]$, the fragment of $\mathrm{MSO}$ up to the quantifier nesting depth $k$. More formally: If $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are two structures of the same purely relational vocabulary, then the duplicator has a winning strategy in the $k$-round $\mathrm{MSO}$ game on $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ iff $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ agree on all sentences of $\mathrm{MSO}[k]$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures
assumptions: $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ are two structures of the same purely relational vocabulary
conclusions: the duplicator has a winning strategy in the $k$-round $\mathrm{MSO}$ game on $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ iff $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ agree on all sentences of $\mathrm{MSO}[k]$
equivalent_conditions: the duplicator has a winning strategy in the $k$-round $\mathrm{MSO}$ game on $\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$
$\mathfrak{A}$ and $\mathfrak{B}$ agree on all sentences of $\mathrm{MSO}[k]$

nodes.name: L-theory of a structure
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be any fragment of second-order logic. The \emph{$\mathcal{L}$-theory} of a structure $\mathfrak{M}$ of a vocabulary $\tau$ is the set of $\tau$-sentences $\varphi$ of $\mathcal{L}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}\models\varphi$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Horizontal and vertical relations H, V
nodes.statement: Define two binary relations $H,V\subseteq\mathbb{N}^2\times\mathbb{N}^2$ as follows. \begin{itemize} \item $H\ =\ \{\ \bigl((i,j),(i+1,j)\bigr)\ |\ i,j\in\mathbb{N}\ \}$. \item $V\ =\ \{\ \bigl((i,j),(i,j+1)\bigr)\ |\ i,j\in\mathbb{N}\ \}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Grid
nodes.statement: We let $\mathfrak{G}$ denote the structure $(\mathbb{N}^2,H,V)$, and call it the \emph{grid}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Horizontal and vertical successor relations
nodes.statement: The relations $H$ and $V$ are called the \emph{horizontal} and \emph{vertical successor relations} of $\mathfrak{G}$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Supergrid
nodes.statement: A \emph{supergrid} is a structure of the vocabulary $\{H,V\}$ that has $\mathfrak{G}$ as a substructure.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Class of supergrids
nodes.statement: We denote the class of supergrids by $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Recurrence relation R
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathfrak{G},R)$ be the expansion of $\mathfrak{G}$, where $R\ =\ \{\ \bigl((0,i),(0,j)\bigr)\in\mathbb{N}^2\times\mathbb{N}^2\ |\ i < j\ \}.$
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: Recurrence grid
nodes.statement: We denote the structure $(\mathfrak{G},R)$ by $\mathfrak{R}$, and call it the \emph{recurrence grid}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures

nodes.name: m x n torus
nodes.statement: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. Define two binary relations $H_{m,n},V_{m,n}\subseteq (m\times n)^2$ as follows. (Note that we define $m = \{0,...,m-1\}$, and analogously for $n$.) \begin{itemize} \item $H_{m,n}=H\upharpoonright (m\times n)^2\cup\{((m-1,i),(0,i))\mid i<n\}$. \item $V_{m,n}=V\upharpoonright (m\times n)^2\cup\{((i,n-1),(i,0))\mid i<m\}$. \end{itemize} We call the structure $(m\times n, H_{m,n},V_{m,n})$ the \emph{$m\times n$ torus} and denote it by $\mathfrak{T}_{m,n}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Logics and structures
nodes.statement_short: The m x n torus: the finite grid on m x n with horizontal/vertical successors wrapping around.

nodes.name: Euclidean space with canonical metric
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathbb{R}^n, d)$ be the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space with the canonical metric $d$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Dimension at least one
nodes.statement: We always assume $n\geq 1$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Euclidean betweenness relation
nodes.statement: We define the ternary Euclidean \emph{betweenness} relation $\beta$ such that $\beta(s,t,u)$ iff \[ d(s,u)=d(s,t)+d(t,u). \]
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Strict betweenness
nodes.statement: By $\beta^*$ we denote the \emph{strict betweenness} relation, i.e., $\beta^*(s,t,u)$ iff $\beta(s,t,u)$ and $s\not=t\not=u$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Collinear points
nodes.statement: We say that the points $s,t,u\in\mathbb{R}^n$ are \emph{collinear} if the disjunction \[ \beta(s,t,u)\vee \beta(s,u,t)\vee \beta(t,s,u) \] holds in $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Collinearity formula
nodes.statement: We define the first-order $\{\beta\}$-formula \[ collinear(x,y,z):=\beta(x,y,z)\vee\beta(x,z,y)\vee\beta(y,x,z). \]
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Geometric betweenness structure (T, beta)
nodes.statement: Below we study geometric betweenness structures of the type $(T,\beta_T)$ where $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\beta_T=\beta\upharpoonright T$. Here $\beta\upharpoonright T$ is the restriction of the betweenness predicate $\beta$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to the set $T$. To simplify notation, we usually refer to these structures by $(T,\beta)$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Line in T
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $\beta$ be the corresponding betweenness relation. We say that $L\subseteq T$ is a \emph{line in $T$} if the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item There exist points $s,t\in L$ such that $s\not= t$. \item For all $s,t,u\in L$, the points $s,t,u$ are collinear. \item Let $s,t\in L$ be points such that $s\not=t$. For all $u\in T$, if $\beta(s,u,t)$ or $\beta(s,t,u)$, then $u\in L$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures
nodes.statement_short: L in T is a line if it has two distinct points, is collinear, and is closed under betweenness from pairs of its points.

nodes.name: Intersecting lines
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be lines in $T$. We say that $L_1$ and $L_2$ \emph{intersect} if $L_1\not=L_2$ and $L_1\cap L_2\neq\emptyset$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Lines intersecting in R^n
nodes.statement: We say that the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ \emph{intersect in $\mathbb{R}^n$} if $L_1\not=L_2$ and $L_1'\cap L_2'\neq\emptyset$, where $L_1',L_2'$ are the lines in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $L_1\subseteq L_1'$ and $L_2\subseteq L_2'$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: m-dimensional flat
nodes.statement: A subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is an \emph{$m$-dimensional flat} of $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $0\leq m\leq n$, if there exists a linearly independent set of $m$ vectors $v_1,\dots,v_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and a vector $h\in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $S$ is the $h$-translated span of the vectors $v_1,\dots,v_m$, in other words \[ S=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid u=h + r_1 v_1 + \dots +r_m v_m,\ r_1,\dots,r_m\in\mathbb{R}\}. \] None of the vectors $v_i$ is allowed to be the zero-vector. (This is relevant in the case where $m=1$.)
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures

nodes.name: Linearly regular m-dimensional flat
nodes.statement: A nonempty set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a \emph{linearly regular $m$-dimensional flat}, where $0\leq m\leq n$, if the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists an $m$-dimensional flat $S$ such that $U\subseteq S$. \item There does not exist any $(m-1)$-dimensional flat $S$ such that $U\subseteq S$. \item $U$ is \emph{linearly complete}, i.e., if $L$ is a line in $U$ and $L'\supseteq L$ the corresponding line in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and if $r\in L'$ is a point in $L'$ and $\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}_+$ a positive real number, then there exists a point $s\in L$ such that $d(s,r) < \epsilon$. Here $d$ is the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}^n$. \item $U$ is \emph{linearly closed}, i.e., if $L_1$ and $L_2$ are lines in $U$ and $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect in $\mathbb{R}^n$, then the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect. In other words, there exists a point $s\in U$ such that $s\in L_1\cap L_2$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures
nodes.statement_short: U lies in an m-flat but no (m-1)-flat, its lines are dense in their real lines, and its lines meeting in R^n meet in U.

nodes.name: Extends linearly in mD
nodes.statement: A set $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ \emph{extends linearly in $mD$}, where $m\leq n$, if there exists a linearly regular $m$-dimensional flat $S$, a positive real number $\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}_+$ and a point $x \in S\cap T$ such that $\{\ u\in S\ |\ d(x,u)<\epsilon\ \}\ \subseteq T.$
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures
nodes.statement_short: T contains a small ball (relative to S) of some linearly regular m-dimensional flat S around a point of T.

nodes.name: Q^2 extends linearly in 2D
nodes.statement: It is easy show that for example $\mathbb{Q}^2$ extends linearly in ${\mathrm{\mathrm{2D}}}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures
conclusions: $\mathbb{Q}^2$ extends linearly in ${\mathrm{\mathrm{2D}}}$

nodes.name: Unary expansion class
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $\beta$ be the corresponding betweenness relation. The class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\{\beta,P\}$, where $P$ is a unary relation symbol, is called \emph{the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$}.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures
also_stated_at: Let $E\bigl((T,\beta)\bigr)$ denote the class of expansions $(T,\beta,P)$ of $(T,\beta)$ with a single unary predicate. The class $E\bigl((T,\beta)\bigr)$ is called the \emph{unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$}.

nodes.name: Unary expansion class with a finite predicate
nodes.statement: By \emph{the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ with a finite predicate}, we mean the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\{\beta,P\}$, where the interpretation of $P$ is a finite set.
nodes.section: 2.3 Geometric affine betweenness structures
nodes.definiendum: unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ with a finite predicate
also_stated_at: Let $F\bigl((T,\beta)\bigr)$ denote the class of structures $(T,\beta,P)$, where the set $P$ is a \emph{finite} subset of $T$.

nodes.name: Tile type
nodes.statement: A function $t:4\longrightarrow\mathbb{N}$ is called a \emph{tile type}.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: TILESYMB
nodes.statement: Define the set $$\mathrm{TILESYMB}\ :=\ \{\ P_t\ |\ t\text{ is a tile type }\ \}$$ of unary relation symbols.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Tile symbols
nodes.statement: The unary relation symbols in the set $\mathrm{TILESYMB}$ are called \emph{tile symbols}.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Colours of a tile symbol
nodes.statement: The numbers $t(i)$ of a tile symbol $P_t$ are the \emph{colours} of $P_t$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Top, right, bottom and left colours
nodes.statement: The number $t(0)$ is the \emph{top colour}, $t(1)$ the \emph{right colour}, $t(2)$ the \emph{bottom colour}, and $t(3)$ the \emph{left colour} of $P_t$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Lexicographic ordering of tile types
nodes.statement: Let $t$ and $s$ be tile types. We define $s < t$, if the tuple $\bigl(s(0),s(1),s(2),s(3)\bigr)$ is situated below the tuple $\bigl(t(0),t(1),t(2),t(3)\bigr)$ with respect to the canonical lexicographic ordering, i.e., $s < t$ if there exists some $i\in 4$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $s(i) < t(i)$, and \item $s(j) = t(j)$ for all $j$ such that $j<i$ and $j\in 4$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Tile type index N(t)
nodes.statement: If $t$ is a tile type, define $N(t)$ to be the number of tile types $s$ such that $s\leq t$. The function $N$ associates each tile type with a unique positive integer.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: T-tilable structure
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. We say that a structure $\mathfrak{A}=(A,V,H)$, where $V,H\subseteq A^2$, is \emph{$T$-tilable}, if there exists an expansion of $\mathfrak{A}$ to the vocabulary $$\{H,V\}\cup\{\ P_t\ |\ P_t\in T\ \}$$ such that the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item Each point of $A$ belongs to the extension of exactly one symbol $P_t$ in $T$. \item If $u H v$ for some points $u,v\in A$, then the right colour of the tile symbol $P_t$ s.t. $P_{t}(u)$ is the same as the left colour of the tile symbol $P_{t'}$ such that $P_{t'}(v)$. \item If $u V v$ for some points $u,v\in A$, then the top colour of the tile symbol $P_t$ s.t. $P_{t}(u)$ is the same as the bottom colour of the tile symbol $P_{t'}$ such that $P_{t'}(v)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings
nodes.statement_short: A structure is T-tilable if each point gets exactly one tile of T with matching colours along H and V edges.

nodes.name: s-recurrently T-tilable grid
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be a tile type such that $P_s\in T$. We say that the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is \emph{$s$-recurrently $T$-tilable}, if there exists an expansion of $\mathfrak{G}$ to the vocabulary $$\{H,V\}\cup\{\ P_t\ |\ P_t\in T\ \}$$ such that the above conditions $(1) - (3)$ hold, and additionally, there exist infinitely many points $(0,i)\in\mathbb{N}^2$ such that $P_s\bigl((0,i)\bigr)$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings
nodes.statement_short: The grid has a T-tiling in which tile P_s occurs infinitely often in the leftmost column.

nodes.name: Input sets F and H
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of finite, nonempty sets $T\subseteq\mathrm{TILESYMB}$, and let $$\mathcal{H}\ :=\ \{\ (t,T)\ |\ T\in\mathcal{F},\ P_t\in T\ \}.$$
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Tiling languages T, R, S
nodes.statement: Define the following languages \begin{align*} \mathcal{T}\ :=&\ \{\ T\in\mathcal{F}\ \mid\ \mathfrak{G}\text{ is $T$-tilable } \},\\ \mathcal{R}\ :=&\ \{\ (t,T)\in\mathcal{H}\ \mid\ \mathfrak{G}\text{ is $t$-recurrently $T$-tilable } \},\\ \mathcal{S}\ :=&\ \{\ T\in \mathcal{F}\ \mid\ \text{ there is a torus $\mathfrak{D}$ which is $T$-tilable }\}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Tiling problem
nodes.statement: The \emph{tiling problem} is the membership problem of the set $\mathcal{T}$ with the input set $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Tilings

nodes.name: Recurrent tiling problem
nodes.statement: The \emph{recurrent tiling problem} is the membership problem of the set $\mathcal{R}$ with the input set $\mathcal{H}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement:
We shall first establish that a set $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is finite iff it is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points of $T$. Recall that an isolated point $u$ of a set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a point such that there exists some open ball $B$ such that $B\cap U =\{u\}$. Assume $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is finite. Since $T$ is finite, we can find a minimum distance between points in the set $T$. Therefore it is clear that each point $t$ in $T$ belongs to some open ball $B$ such that $B\cap T = \{t\}$, and hence $T$ consists of isolated points. Similarly, since $T$ is finite, each point $b$ in the complement of $T$ has some minimum distance to the points of $T$, and therefore $b$ belongs to some open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus T$. Hence the set $T$ is the complement of the union of open balls $B$ such that $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus T$, and therefore $T$ is closed. Finally, since $T$ is finite, we can find a maximum distance between the points in $T$, and therefore $T$ is bounded. Assume then that $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points of $T$. Since $T$ consists of isolated points, it has an open cover $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathrm{Pow}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that each set in $\mathcal{C}$ contains exactly one point $t\in T$. The set $\mathcal{C}$ is an open cover of $T$, and by the Heine-Borel theorem, there exists a finite subcover $\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of the set $T$. Since $\mathcal{D}$ is finite and each set in $\mathcal{D}$ contains exactly one point of $T$, the set $T$ must also be finite. We then conclude the proof by establishing that there exists a first-order formula $\varphi(P)$ stating that the unary predicate $P$ is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points. We will first define a formula $\mathit{parallel}(x,y,t,k)$ stating that the lines defined by $x,y$ and $t,k$ are parallel in $(\mathbb{R}^n, eta)$. We define  egin{align*} &\mathit{parallel}(x,y,t,k):= x
eq y\wedge t
eq k \wedge \Big((\mathit{collinear}(x,y,t)\wedge \mathit{collinear}(x,y,k))\ &\quad\vee  ig(
eg\exists z(\mathit{collinear}(x,y,z)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(t,k,z))\ &\quad\quad\wedge \exists z_1 z_2(x
eq z_1\wedge\mathit{collinear}(x,y,z_1)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(x,t,z_2)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(z_1,z_2,k))\,  ig)\Big). \end{align*} We will then define first-order $\{ eta\}$-formulae $\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)$ and $\mathit{flat}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z)$ using simultaneous recursion. The first formula states that the vectors corresponding to the pairs $(x_0,x_i)$, $1\leq i\leq k$, form a basis of a $k$-dimensional flat. The second formula states that the point $z$ is in the span of the basis defined by the vectors $(x_0,x_i)$, the origin being $x_0$. First define $\mathit{basis}_0(x_0):= x_0=x_0$ and $\mathit{flat}_0(x_0,z):= x_0=z$. Then define $\mathit{flat}_k$ and $\mathit{basis_k}$ recursively in the following way.  egin{align*} &\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k):=\mathit{basis}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1})\wedge 
eg \mathit{flat}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},x_k),\ &\mathit{flat}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z):=\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)\ &\quad\wedge \exists y_0\dots \exists y_k\Big(y_0=x_0 \wedge y_k=z \wedge igwedge_{i\, \leq\, k-1}  ig(y_i=y_{i+1}\vee\mathit{parallel}(x_0,x_{i+1},y_i,y_{i+1}) ig)\Big). \end{align*} We then define a first-order $\{ eta,P\}$-formula $\mathit{sepr}(x,P)$ asserting that $x$ belongs to an open ball $B$ such that each point in $B\setminus\{x\}$ belongs to the complement of $P$. The idea is to state that there exist $n+1$ points $x_0,\dots,x_n$ that form an \emph{$n$-dimensional triangle} around $x$, and every point contained in the triangle (with $x$ being a possible exception) belongs to the complement of $P$. Every open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is contained in some $n$-dimensional triangle in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and vice versa. We will recursively define first-order formulae $\mathit{opentriangle}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z)$ stating that $z$ is properly inside a $k$-dimensional triangle defined by $x_0,\dots,x_k$, see Figure ef{fig:opentriangle}. First define $\mathit{opentriangle}_1(x_0,x_1,z):= eta^*(x_0,z,x_1)$, and then define  egin{align*} &\mathit{opentriangle}_{k}(x_0,\dots,x_k,z):=\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)\ &\quad\wedge \exists y ig(\mathit{opentriangle}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},y)\wedge  eta^*(y,z,x_k) ig). \end{align*}  egin{figure} \centering \includegraphics[scale=2]{finiteness2} \caption{The figure shows how the formula $\mathit{opentriangle}_2(y,z,u,x)$ is interpreted.} \end{figure}We are now ready to define $\mathit{sepr}(x,P)$. Let  egin{multline*} \mathit{sepr}(x,P) := \exists x_0\dots \exists x_n\Bigl(\mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots, x_n,x)\ \wedge  orall y  ig((\mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n,y)\wedge y
eq x)ightarrow 
eg Py ig)\Bigr). \end{multline*} Now, the sentence $\varphi_1:= orall x igl(
eg Px\ ightarrow\ \mathit{sepr}(x,P) igr)$ states that each point in the complement of $P$ is contained in an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P$. The sentence therefore states that the complement of $P$ is a union of open balls. Since the set of unions of open balls is exactly the same as the set of open sets, the sentence states that $P$ is closed. The sentence $\varphi_2:= orall x igl(Px\ ightarrow\ \mathit{sepr}(x,P) igr)$ clearly states that $P$ consists of isolated points. Finally, in order to state that $P$ is bounded, we define a formula asserting that there exist points $x_0,\dots,x_n$ that form an n-dimensional triangle around $P$.  egin{multline*} \varphi_3:=\exists x_0\dots \exists x_n\Bigl(\mathit{basis}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n) \wedge  orall y igl(Pyightarrow \mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n,y) igr)\Bigr) \end{multline*} The conjunction $\varphi_1\wedge\varphi_2\wedge\varphi_3$ states that $P$ is finite.

nodes.name: Sequence in T
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Let $L$ be a line in $T$. Any nonempty subset $Q$ of $L$ is called a \emph{sequence} in $T$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences

nodes.name: Linearly E-connected points
nodes.statement: Let $E\subseteq T$ and $s,t\in T$. If $s\not=t$ and if $u\in E$ for all points $u\in T$ such that $\beta^*(s,u,t)$, we say that the points $s$ and $t$ are \emph{linearly $E$-connected} (in $(T,\beta)$).
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences

nodes.name: Linearly disconnected points
nodes.statement: If there exists a point $v\in T\setminus E$ such that $\beta^*(s,v,t)$, we say that $s$ and $t$ are \emph{linearly disconnected with respect to $E$} (in $(T,\beta)$).
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences

nodes.name: Discretely spaced sequence
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a sequence in $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Suppose that for each $s,t\in Q$ such that $s\not=t$, there exists a point $u\in T\setminus\{s\}$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\beta(s,u,t)$ and \item $\forall r\, \in\, T\ \bigl(\, \beta^*(s,r,u)\rightarrow r\not\in Q\, \bigr)$, i.e., the points $s$ and $u$ are linearly $(T\setminus Q)$-connected. \end{enumerate} Then we call $Q$ a $\emph{discretely spaced sequence in T}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Each point of Q has, towards any other point of Q, a nearby point u with no Q-points strictly between them.
nodes.label: discretelyspaceddfn

nodes.name: Discretely infinite sequence; base point
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a discretely spaced sequence in $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Assume that there exists a point $s\in Q$ such that for each point $u\in Q$, there exists a point $v\in Q\setminus\{u\}$ such that $\beta(s,u,v)$. Then we call the sequence $Q$ a \emph{discretely infinite sequence in $T$}. The point $s$ is called a \emph{base point} of $Q$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.label: discretelyinfinitedfn

nodes.name: Sequence with a zero; zero-point
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a sequence in $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Let $s\in Q$ be a point such that there do not exist points $u,v\in Q\setminus\{s\}$ such that $\beta(u,s,v)$. Then we call $Q$ a \emph{sequence in $T$ with a zero}. The point $s$ is a \emph{zero-point of $Q$}. Notice that $Q$ may have up to two zero-points.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.label: sequencewithzero

nodes.name: A discretely infinite sequence has at most one zero-point
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that a discretely infinite sequence has at most one zero-point.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
assumptions: a discretely infinite sequence
conclusions: has at most one zero-point

nodes.name: omega-like sequence
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a discretely infinite sequence in $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with a zero. Assume that for each $r\in T$ such that there exist points $s,u\in Q\setminus\{r\}$ with $\beta(s,r,u)$, there also exist points $s',u'\in Q\setminus\{r\}$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\beta(s',r,u')$ and \item $\forall v\, \in\, T\setminus\{r\}\ \bigl(\, \beta^*(s',v,u')\rightarrow v\not\in Q\, \bigr)$. \end{enumerate} Then we call $Q$ an \emph{$\omega$-like sequence in $T$} (cf. Lemma \ref{nonstandardmodelsexcluded}).
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.genus: discretely infinite sequence in $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with a zero
nodes.statement_short: A discretely infinite sequence with a zero in which every point of T between two points of Q lies between two Q-neighbours.
nodes.label: omegalikedfn

nodes.name: First-order definability of omega-like sequences
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a unary relation symbol. There is a first-order sentence $\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ of the vocabulary $\{\beta,P\}$ such that for every $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and for every expansion $(T,\beta,P)$ of $(T,\beta)$, we have $(T,\beta,P)\models\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ if and only if the interpretation of $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence in $T$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
assumptions: Let $P$ be a unary relation symbol.
conclusions: There is a first-order sentence $\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ of the vocabulary $\{\beta,P\}$ such that for every $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and for every expansion $(T,\beta,P)$ of $(T,\beta)$, we have $(T,\beta,P)\models\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ if and only if the interpretation of $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence in $T$.
nodes.label: omegalikesequencedefinability

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement: Define \[ \mathit{sequence}(P):=\exists x\, Px\, \wedge\, \forall x\forall y\forall z\, \bigl(Px\wedge Py \wedge Pz\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{collinear}(x,y,z)\bigr). \] The formula $sequence(P)$ states that $P$ is a sequence. By inspection of Definition \ref{discretelyspaceddfn}, it is easy to see that there is a first-order formula $\psi$ such that the conjunction $sequence(P)\wedge\psi$ states that $P$ is a discretely spaced sequence. Continuing this trend, it is straightforward to observe that Definitions \ref{discretelyinfinitedfn}, \ref{sequencewithzero} and \ref{omegalikedfn} specify first-order properties, and therefore there exists a first-order formula $\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ stating that $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Write sequence(P) explicitly; the remaining defining conditions are first-order by inspection.

nodes.name: Adjacent points; successor relation of a sequence
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a sequence in $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $s,t\in P$. The points $s,t$ are called \emph{adjacent} with respect to $P$, if the points are linearly $(T\setminus P)$-connected. Let $E\subseteq P\times P$ be the set of pairs $(u,v)$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $u$ and $v$ are adjacent with respect to $P$, and \item $\beta(z,u,v)$ for some zero-point $z$ of $P$. \end{enumerate} We call $E$ the \emph{successor relation} of $P$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.label: successordefinition

nodes.name: Successor relation of N
nodes.statement: We let $\mathit{succ}$ denote the successor relation of $\mathbb{N}$, i.e., $\mathit{succ}:=\{\ (i,j)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\ |\ i+1 = j\ \}.$
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences

nodes.name: Omega-like sequences exclude nonstandard models
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an $\omega$-like sequence in $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $E$ the successor relation of $P$. There is an embedding from $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$ such that $0\in\mathbb{N}$ maps to the zero-point of $P$. If $T=\mathbb{R}^n$, then $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ is isomorphic to $(P,E)$.

$T=\mathbb{R}^n$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement:
We denote by $i_0$ the unique zero-point of $P$. Since $P$ is a discretely infinite sequence, it has a base point. Clearly $i_0$ has to be the only base point of $P$. It is straightforward to establish that since $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence with the base point $i_0$, there exists a sequence $(a_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ of points $a_i\in P$ such that $i_0=a_0$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the unique $E$-successor of $a_{i}$ for all $i\in \mathbb{N}$. Define the function $h:\mathbb{N}ightarrow P$ such that $h(i) = a_i$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $h$ is an embedding of $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$. Assume then that $T=\mathbb{R}^n$. We shall show that the function $h:\mathbb{N}\longrightarrow P$ is a surjection. Let $d$ denote the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}$, and let $d_R$ be the restriction of the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to the line $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $P\subseteq R$. Let $g:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow R$ be the isometry from $(\mathbb{R},d)$ to $(R,d_R)$ such that $g(0) = i_0 = h(0)$ and such that for all $r\in\mathit{ran}(h)$, we have $ eta igl(i_0,g(1),r igr)$ or $ eta igl(i_0,r,g(1) igr)$. Let $(R,\leq^R)$ be the structure, where $$\leq^{R}\ =\ \{\ (u,v)\in R	imes R\ |\ g^{-1}(u)\, \leq^{\mathbb{R}}\, g^{-1}(v)\ \}.$$ If $\mathit{ran}(h)$ is not bounded from above w.r.t. $\leq^R$, then $h$ must be a surjection. Therefore assume that $\mathit{ran}(h)$ is bounded above. By the Dedekind completeness of the reals, there exists a least upper bound $s\in R$ of $\mathit{ran}(h)$ w.r.t. $\leq^R$. Notice that since $h$ is an embedding of $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$, we have $s
ot\in\mathit{ran}(h)$. Due to the definition of $E$, it is sufficient to show that $\{\, t\in P\ |\ s\leq^R t\ \} = \emptyset$ in order to conclude that $h$ maps onto $P$. Assume that the least upper bound $s$ belongs to the set $P$. Since $P$ is a discretely spaced sequence, there is a point $u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{s\}$ such that $ eta(s,u,i_0)$ and $$ orall r\in\mathbb{R}^n  igl( eta^*(s,r,u) ightarrow r
ot\in P igl).$$ Now $u<^R s$ and the points $u$ and $s$ are linearly $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P)$-connected, implying that $s$ cannot be the least upper bound of $\mathit{ran}(h)$. This is a contradiction. Therefore $s
ot\in P$. Assume, ad absurdum, that there exists a point $t\in P$ such that $ eta(i_0,s,t)$. Now, since $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence, there exists points $u',v'\in P\setminus\{s\}$ such that $ eta(u',s,v')$ and $$ orall r\in \mathbb{R}^n igl( eta^*(u',r,v')ightarrow r
ot\in P igr).$$ We have $ eta(s,u',i_0)$ or $ eta(s,v',i_0)$. Assume, by symmetry, that $ eta(s,u',i_0)$. Now $u'<^R s$, and the points $u'$ and $s$ are linearly $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P)$-connected. Hence, since $s
ot\in \mathit{ran}(h)$, we conclude that $s$ is not the least upper bound of $\mathit{ran}(h)$. This is a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Build the embedding by iterating successors from the zero-point; for T = R^n, a least upper bound of the range contradicts discrete spacing and omega-likeness.

nodes.name: omega-like sequence with an endpoint
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be an $\omega$-like sequence in $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $q_0$ be the unique zero-point of $Q$. Assume there exists a point $q_e\in T\setminus Q$ such that $\beta(q_0,q,q_e)$ holds for all $q\in Q$. We call $Q\cup\{q_e\}$ \emph{an $\omega$-like sequence with an endpoint in $T$}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class

nodes.name: Endpoint
nodes.statement: The point $q_e$ is the \emph{endpoint of $Q\cup\{q_e\}$}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class

nodes.name: Characterisation of the endpoint
nodes.statement: Notice that the endpoint $q_e$ is the only point $x$ in $Q\cup\{q_e\}$ such that the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item There do not exist points $s,t\in Q\cup\{q_e\}$ such that $\beta^*(s,x,t)$. \item $\forall y z \in Q\cup\{q_e\}\Bigl(\, \beta^*(x,y,z)\rightarrow \exists v\in Q\cup\{q_e\}\beta^*(x,v,y)\Bigr)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
conclusions: the endpoint $q_e$ is the only point $x$ in $Q\cup\{q_e\}$ such that the following conditions hold.

nodes.name: Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Let $P\subseteq T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $p_0,p_x,p_y\in P$. We call the structure $$\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$$ a \emph{Cartesian frame} with domain $T$, if the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item The points $p_0$, $p_x$ and $p_y$ are not collinear, i.e., $\mathit{collinear}(p_0,p_x,p_y)$ does not hold in the structure $\mathfrak{C}$. \item The set $$P_x=\{\ u\in P\mid \mathit{collinear}(p_0,u,p_x) \text{ holds in }\mathfrak{C}\ \}$$ is an $\omega$-like sequence with an endpoint in $T$. The point $p_x$ is the endpoint of $P_x$. \item The set $$P_y=\{\ u\in P\mid \mathit{collinear}(p_0,u,p_y)\text{ holds in }\mathfrak{C}\ \}$$ is an $\omega$-like sequence with an endpoint in $T$. The point $p_y$ is the endpoint of $P_y$. \item The point $p_0$ is the zero-point of both $P_x\setminus\{p_x\}$ and $P_y\setminus\{p_y\}$. \item For each point $p\in P_x\setminus\{p_x\}$ and $q\in P_y\setminus\{p_ y\}$, the unique lines $L_p$ and $L_q$ in $T$ such that $p,p_y\in L_p$ and $q,p_x\in L_q$, intersect. In other words, there exists a point $u\in T$ that lies on both lines $L_p$ and $L_q$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: (T,beta,P,p0,px,py): two omega-like sequences with endpoints along non-collinear axes from p0, whose connecting lines always intersect in T.

nodes.name: Intersection point of a Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be a Cartesian frame. Let $p\in P_x\setminus\{p_x\}$ and $q\in P_y\setminus\{p_y\}$ be points and $L_p$ and $L_q$ the lines in $T$ such that $p,p_y\in L_p$ and $q,p_x\in L_q$. The point $u\in T$ that lies on both lines $L_p$ and $L_q$ is called---rather suggestively---the \emph{intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding to the pair $(p,q)$}. A point $u\in T$ is called an \emph{intersection point} of the Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$, if it is an intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding some pair $(p,q)$, where $p\in P_x\setminus\{p_x\}$ and $q\in P_y\setminus\{p_y\}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.label: intersectionpointdefinition

nodes.name: Diagonal successor
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be a Cartesian frame. Recall Definition \ref{successordefinition}. Let $E_x$ be the successor relation of the $\omega$-like sequence $P_x\setminus\{p_x\}$ and $E_y$ the successor relation of $P_y\setminus\{p_y\}$. Let $p,p',q,q'$ be points such that $(p,p')\in E_x$ and $(q,q')\in E_y$. Let $u$ be the intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding to $(p,q)$ and $v$ the intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding to $(p',q')$. We say that $v$ is the \emph{diagonal successor} of $u$ in $\mathfrak{C}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.label: diagonalsuccessordefinition

nodes.name: S-labelled Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Recall the function $N$ that associates each tile type $t$ with the unique positive integer $N(t)$ (see the Preliminaries section). Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be a Cartesian frame and let $S\not=\emptyset$ be a finite set of tile symbols. We call $\mathfrak{C}$ an \emph{$S$-labelled Cartesian frame} if the number of points in $P$ strictly between any intersection point $u$ of $\mathfrak{C}$ and its diagonal successor $v$ is in the set $\{N(t)\mid P_t\in S\}$. If $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $S\not=\emptyset$ is a finite set of tile symbols, we let $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$ denote the class of exactly all $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with domain $T$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: A Cartesian frame where the number of P-points between each intersection point and its diagonal successor codes a tile N(t) of S.

nodes.name: First-order definability of S-labelled Cartesian frames
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq 2$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the class of all expansions $(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a unary relation $P$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y$. There is a computable function associating each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\{\beta, P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$-sentence $\varphi_\mathit{Cf}^S$ that defines the class of $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class $\mathcal{C}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
assumptions: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq 2$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the class of all expansions $(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a unary relation $P$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y$.
conclusions: There is a computable function associating each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\{\beta, P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$-sentence $\varphi_\mathit{Cf}^S$ that defines the class of $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class $\mathcal{C}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.12
nodes.statement: Straightforward by virtue of Lemma \ref{omegalikesequencedefinability}.

nodes.statement_short: Follows from FO definability of omega-like sequences (Lemma 4.5).

nodes.name: Class of S-labelled grids
nodes.statement: Let $S\not=\emptyset$ be a finite set of tile symbols. We let $\mathfrak{G}_S$ denote the class of structures $\mathfrak{A}$ that satisfy the following conditions. \begin{enumerate} \item The structure $\mathfrak{A}$ is an expansion of the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ to the vocabulary $\{V,H\}\cup S$. \item Each point in the domain of $\mathfrak{A}$ is in the extension of exactly one predicate symbol $P_t\in S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class

nodes.name: S-labelled grids
nodes.statement: Structures in the class $\mathfrak{G}_S$ are called \emph{$S$-labelled grids}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class

nodes.name: Class of S-labelled supergrids
nodes.statement: Similarly, we let $\mathcal{G}_S$ denote the class of structures $\mathfrak{A}$ that satisfy the following conditions. \begin{enumerate} \item The structure $\mathfrak{A}$ is an expansion of some supergrid to the vocabulary $\{V,H\}\cup S$. \item Each point in the domain of $\mathfrak{A}$ is in the extension of exactly one predicate symbol $P_t\in S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class

nodes.name: S-labelled supergrids
nodes.statement: Structures in the class $\mathcal{G}_S$ are called \emph{$S$-labelled supergrids}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class

nodes.name: S-labelled recurrence grids
nodes.statement: The class of \emph{$S$-labelled recurrence grids} is defined in the obvious way.

nodes.name: Interpretability of labelled supergrids in labelled Cartesian frames
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a set that extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$. There is a computable function $I$ such that for each finite set of tile symbols $S\not=\emptyset$, there exists some class $\mathcal{G}(T,S)\supseteq \mathfrak{G}_S$ of $S$-labelled supergrids such that the function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{G}(T,S)$ in $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
assumptions: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a set that extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$.
conclusions: There is a computable function $I$ such that for each finite set of tile symbols $S\not=\emptyset$, there exists some class $\mathcal{G}(T,S)\supseteq \mathfrak{G}_S$ of $S$-labelled supergrids such that the function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{G}(T,S)$ in $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$.

assumptions: Let $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a set and $\beta$ be the corresponding betweenness relation.
Assume that $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$.
conclusions: The first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ is $\Sigma_1^0$-hard.

The first-order theory of the class of expansions of $(T,\beta)$ with a single unary predicate is $\Sigma_1^0$-hard.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.15
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma = \{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of supergrids, and let $\tau = \{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled Cartesian frames. By Lemma \ref{boxedcartesianpicturesdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$ denote such a sentence. By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_{S}$ such that a structure $\mathfrak{A}$ of the vocabulary $\sigma$ is $S$-tilable if and only if there is an expansion $\mathfrak{A}^*$ of the structure $\mathfrak{A}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{A}^*\models\varphi_{S}$. Now recall Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}. By Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}, since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, there exists a computable function $I$ such that for each input $S$ to the tiling problem, the function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of some class $\mathcal{G}(T,S)\supseteq \mathfrak{G}_S$ of $S$-labelled supergrids in the class $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$ of all $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$. Let $S$ be an input to the tiling problem. Define the $\tau$-sentence \[ \psi_{S}\, :=\, \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S\, \wedge\, I(\, \varphi_{S}\, ). \] We will prove that for each input $S$ to the tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There \emph{exists} an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$. \item The grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate} Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the \emph{complement problem} of the tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$. Since the tiling problem is $\Pi_1^0$-complete, its complement problem is $\Sigma_1^0$-complete.\footnote{It is of course a well-known triviality that the complement $\overline{A}$ of a problem $A$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-hard if $A$ is $\Pi^0_1$-hard. Choose an arbitrary problem $B\in \Sigma^0_1$. Therefore $\overline{B}\in\Pi^0_1$. By the hardness of $A$, there is a computable reduction $f$ such that $x\in\overline{B}\Leftrightarrow f(x)\in A$, whence $x\in B\Leftrightarrow f(x)\in \overline{A}$.} Let $S$ be an input to the tiling problem. Assume first that the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{G}^*$ of the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ to the vocabulary $\{H,V\}\, \cup\, S$ such that $\mathfrak{G}^*\models\varphi_{S}$. Now since $\mathfrak{G}^*\in\mathfrak{G}_S\subseteq\mathcal{G}(T,S)$, by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} there exists an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models I(\varphi_{S})$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame, we have $\mathfrak{C}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S\wedge I(\varphi_{S})$. Hence the Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\psi_S$. For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that we have $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models I(\varphi_{S})$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame with the domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models I(\varphi_{S})$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_{S}$ for some $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{G}(T,S)$. Thus there exists a supergrid that is $S$-tilable. Hence the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable.

nodes.statement_short: Reduction from the complement of the tiling problem: conjoin the frame-defining sentence with the interpreted tiling sentence; prove equisatisfiability both ways.

nodes.name: Extending linearly in 1D does not suffice
nodes.statement: As a partial converse to Theorem \ref{infinitelemma}, we note that $T$ extending linearly $\mathrm{1D}$ is not a sufficient condition for undecidability of even the monadic $\Pi_1^1$-theory of $(T,\beta)$. For instance, the monadic $\Pi_1^1$-theory of $(\mathbb{R},\beta)$ is decidable; this follows trivially from the known result that the monadic $\Pi_1^1$-theory $(\mathbb{R},\leq)$ is decidable, see \cite{Burgess}. Also the monadic $\Pi_1^1$-theory of $(\mathbb{Q},\beta)$ is decidable since the $\mathrm{MSO}$-theory of $(\mathbb{Q},\leq)$ is decidable \cite{Rabin:1969}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Linear extension in 1D is not enough: the monadic Pi^1_1 theories of (R,beta) and (Q,beta) are decidable by Burgess and Rabin.
also_stated_at: We observe that $T$ extending linearly in $\mathrm{1D}$ (see Section \ref{structures} for the definition) is not a sufficient condition for undecidability of the $\mathrm{FO}$-theory of $E\bigl((T,\beta)\bigr)$.

nodes.name: Pi^1_1-hardness for (R^n, beta)

nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
assumptions: Let $n\geq 2$ be an integer.
conclusions: The first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$ is $\Pi_1^1$-hard.
also_stated_at: In addition, we establish that for all $n\geq 2$, the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$ is $\Pi_1^1$-hard, and therefore not even arithmetical.
We have established that for $n\geq 2$, the first-order theory of the class of all expansions of $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$ with a single unary predicate is highly undecidable ($\Pi_1^1$-hard).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.16
nodes.statement: The proof is essentially the same as the proof of Theorem \ref{infinitelemma}. The main difference is that we use Lemma \ref{recurrencegridinterpr} and interpret a class of labelled recurrence grids instead of a class of labelled supergrids, and hence obtain a reduction from the recurrent tiling problem instead of the ordinary tiling problem. Thereby we establish $\Pi^1_1$-hardness instead of $\Sigma_1^0$-hardness. Due to the recurrence condition of the recurrent tiling problem, the result of Lemma \ref{nonstandardmodelsexcluded} that there is an isomorphism from $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ to $(P,E)$---rather than an embedding---is essential.

nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a subset of $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. We say that $Q$ is a \emph{finite sequence} in $T$ if $Q$ is a finite nonempty set and the points in $Q$ are collinear.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate

nodes.name: Finite Cartesian frame; m x k Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $\beta$ be the corresponding betweenness relation. Let $P\subseteq T$ be a finite set, and let $p_0,p_x,p_y\in P$. We call the structure \[ \mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y) \] \emph{a finite Cartesian frame} with domain $T$ if the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item The points $p_0$, $p_x$ and $p_y$ are not collinear. \item For each point $p\in P$ and $q\in P$ such that $\beta^*(p_0,p,p_x)$ and $\beta^*(p_0,q,p_y)$ hold in $\mathfrak{C}$, the unique lines $L_p$ and $L_q$ in $T$ such that $p,p_y\in L_p$ and $q,p_x\in L_q$, intersect. In other words, there exists a point $u\in T$ that lies on both lines $L_p$ and $L_q$. \end{enumerate} If $m$ and $k$ are positive integers such that \begin{align*} &\lvert \{u\in P\mid \beta(p_0,u,p_x) \text{ holds in }\mathfrak{C}\}\rvert=m+2\text{ and}\\ &\lvert \{u\in P\mid \beta(p_0,u,p_y) \text{ holds in }\mathfrak{C}\}\rvert=k+2, \end{align*} we call $(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ an \emph{$m\times k$ Cartesian frame} with domain $T$.

nodes.statement_short: A finite P with non-collinear p0,px,py whose connecting lines intersect in T; m x k counts axis points.

nodes.name: Intersection point of a finite Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be a finite Cartesian frame. Let $p,q\in P$, $p\neq p_x$, $q\neq p_y$, be points such that $\beta(p_0,p,p_x)$ and $\beta(p_0,q,p_y)$ hold in $\mathfrak{C}$. Let $L_p$ and $L_q$ be the lines in $T$ such that $p,p_y\in L_p$ and $q,p_x\in L_q$. The point $u\in T$ that lies on both lines $L_p$ and $L_q$ is called the \emph{intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding to the pair $(p,q)$}. A point $u\in T$ is called an \emph{intersection point} of the finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$, if it is an intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding to some pair $(p,q)$.

nodes.name: Diagonal successor in a finite Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be a finite Cartesian frame. Let $p,p',q,q'\in P$ be points such that the following conditions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item $\beta(p_0,p,p')$ and $\beta^*(p,p',p_x)$ hold in $\mathfrak{C}$. \item $\beta(p_0,q,q')$ and $\beta^*(q,q',p_y)$ hold in $\mathfrak{C}$. \item There does not exist a point $u\in P$ such that $\beta^*(p,u,p')$ or $\beta^*(q,u,q')$ holds in $\mathfrak{C}$. \end{enumerate} Let $u$ be the intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ corresponding to $(p,q)$ and $v$ the intersection point of $\mathfrak{C}$ correponding to $(p',q')$. We say that $v$ is the \emph{diagonal successor} of $u$ in $\mathfrak{C}$.

nodes.name: S-labelled finite Cartesian frame
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be a finite Cartesian frame and let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. We call $\mathfrak{C}$ an \emph{$S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame} if the number of points in $P$ strictly between any intersection point $u$ of $\mathfrak{C}$ and its diagonal successor $v$ is in the set $\{N(P_t)\mid P_t\in S\}$. We let $\mathcal{C}^{fin}(T,S)$ denote \emph{the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with domain $T$}.

nodes.name: First-order definability of S-labelled finite Cartesian frames
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq 2$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the class of all expansions $(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P$ and constants $p_0$, $p_x$ and $p_y$. There is a computable function associating each finite nonempty set of tile symbols $S$ with a first-order $\{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$-sentence $\varphi_{fCf}^S$ that defines the class $\mathcal{C}^\mathit{fin}(T,S)$ with respect to the class $\mathcal{C}$.

In the definitions of the new formulae, we shall make use of the old formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_{H}$, $\varphi_{V}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}$. We define  egin{align*} \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)&\ :=\ \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\wedge \exists x\exists y igl(\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(x)\wedge \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(y)\wedge \varphi_H(u,x)\wedge \varphi_V(u,y)  igr),\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(u,v)&\ :=\ \varphi_H(u,v) \vee\Big( eta(p_0,v,p_y)\wedge eta(v,u,p_x)\wedge  orall x ig( eta^*(u,x,p_x)ightarrow
eg\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^{\mathit{fin}}(x) ig)\Big),\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(u,v)&\ :=\ \varphi_V(u,v) \vee\Big( eta(p_0,v,p_x)\wedge eta(v,u,p_y)\wedge  orall x ig( eta^*(u,x,p_y)ightarrow
eg\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^{\mathit{fin}}(x) ig)\Big),\ \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(u)&\ :=\ \varphi_{P_t}(u)	ext{ for each }P_t\in S. \end{align*} Let $F_\mathfrak{C}:=\{u\in T \mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_{Dom}(u)\}$. Define the structure $$\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}= igl(F_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}, (P_t^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S} igr),$$ where  egin{align*} H^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{(u,v)\in F_\mathfrak{C}	imes F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(u,v)\}, \ V^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{(u,v)\in F_\mathfrak{C}	imes F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(u,v)\}, \ P_t^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{u\in F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(u)\}, \end{align*} for all $P_t\in S$. nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.7
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma=\{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of tori, and let $\tau=\{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled finite Cartesian frames. By Lemma \ref{finitedefinable}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi^S_{\mathit{fCf}}$ denote such a sentence. By Lemma \ref{torusinterpretablelemma}, there is a computable function $J$ such that for all inputs $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with domain $T$. By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_S$ such that for all tori $\mathfrak{B}$, the torus $\mathfrak{B}$ is $S$-tilable iff there is an expansion $\mathfrak{B}^*$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^*\models\varphi_{S}$. Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. Define the first-order $\tau$-sentence \[ \gamma_S:=\varphi_{\mathit{fCf}}^S\wedge J(\varphi_S). \] We will prove that for each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. \item There exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate} Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the complement problem of the periodic tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ with a finite predicate. Since the periodic tiling problem is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete, its complement problem is $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Let $S$ be an input to the periodic tiling problem. First assume that there exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{T}^*$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{T}^*\models \varphi_S$. Since the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$, and since $\mathfrak{T}^*\models\varphi_S$, it follows by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that there exists an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models J(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame, we have that $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}\wedge J(\varphi_S)$. Hence the finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\gamma_S$. For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models J_S(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame with domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models J(\varphi_S)$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_S$ holds for some $S$-labelled torus $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma} there exists a torus that is $S$-tilable.

nodes.name: Examples of structures extending linearly in 2D
nodes.statement: Geometric structures that extend linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$ include, for example, the rational plane $(\mathbb{Q}^2,\beta)$ and the real unit rectangle $([0,1]^2,\beta)$, to name a few.
nodes.section: 6 Conclusions

nodes.name: Extension to restricted expansion classes
nodes.statement: The techniques used in the proofs can be easily modified to yield undecidability of first-order theories of a significant variety of natural restricted expansion classes of the affine real plane $(\mathbb{R}^2,\beta)$, such as those with a unary predicate denoting a polygon, a finite union of closed rectangles, and a semialgebraic set, for example.
nodes.section: 6 Conclusions
also_stated_at: The torus tiling argument can easily be adapted to deal with various different kinds of natural restricted expansion classes of geometric structures $(T,\beta)$. These include classes with a unary predicate denoting---to name a few examples---a polygon, a finite union of closed rectangles, and a semialgebraic set (see \cite{realalgebraicgeometry} for the definition).

nodes.name: Infinity is forall-WMSO definable but not MSO definable (EF game)
nodes.statement: It is easy to observe that $\forall\mathrm{WMSO}\not\leq\mathrm{MSO}$: consider the sentence $\forall X\exists y\, \neg Xy$. This $\forall\mathrm{WMSO}$ sentence is true in a model iff the domain of the model is infinite. A straightforward monadic second-order Ehrenfeucht-Fra\"{i}ss\'{e} game argument can be used to establish that infinity is not expressible by any $\mathrm{MSO}$ sentence.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Infinity is forall-WMSO definable but not MSO definable (EF game).

nodes.name: Consider (R,<) and (Q,<)
nodes.statement: To show that $\forall\mathrm{MSO}\not\leq\mathrm{WMSO}$, consider the structures $(\mathbb{R},<)$ and $(\mathbb{Q},<)$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Consider (R,<) and (Q,<).

nodes.name: A forall-MSO completeness sentence separates them
nodes.statement: The structures can be separated by a sentence of $\forall\mathrm{MSO}$ stating that every subset bounded from above has a least upper bound.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: A forall-MSO completeness sentence separates them.

nodes.name: Use the weak EF game with finite sets, which characterizes WMSO
nodes.statement: To see that the two structures cannot be separated by any sentence of $\mathrm{WMSO}$, consider the variant of the $\mathrm{MSO}$ Ehrenfeucht-Fra\"{i}ss\'{e} game where the players choose \emph{finite sets} in addition to domain elements. It is easy to establish that this game characterizes the expressivity of $\mathrm{WMSO}$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Use the weak EF game with finite sets, which characterizes WMSO.

nodes.name: Duplicator wins by extending the folklore first-order strategy
nodes.statement: To see that the duplicator has a winning strategy in a game of any finite length played on the structures $(\mathbb{R},<)$ and $(\mathbb{Q},<)$, we devise an extension of the folklore winning strategy in the corresponding first-order game. Firstly, the duplicator can obviously always pick an element whose betweenness configuration corresponds exactly to that of the element picked by the spoiler.
