nodes.statement_short: Duplicator wins by extending the folklore first-order strategy.

nodes.name: Reduce finiteness to closed, bounded and discrete
nodes.statement: We shall first establish that a set $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is finite iff it is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points of $T$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce finiteness to closed, bounded and discrete.

nodes.name: Recall isolated points
nodes.statement: Recall that an isolated point $u$ of a set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a point such that there exists some open ball $B$ such that $B\cap U =\{u\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Recall isolated points.

nodes.name: Finite T: minimum distances give isolation and open balls in the complement
nodes.statement: Assume $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is finite. Since $T$ is finite, we can find a minimum distance between points in the set $T$. Therefore it is clear that each point $t$ in $T$ belongs to some open ball $B$ such that $B\cap T = \{t\}$, and hence $T$ consists of isolated points. Similarly, since $T$ is finite, each point $b$ in the complement of $T$ has some minimum distance to the points of $T$, and therefore $b$ belongs to some open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus T$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Finite T: minimum distances give isolation and open balls in the complement.

nodes.name: So T is closed
nodes.statement: Hence the set $T$ is the complement of the union of open balls $B$ such that $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus T$, and therefore $T$ is closed.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: So T is closed.

nodes.name: Finite T is bounded
nodes.statement: Finally, since $T$ is finite, we can find a maximum distance between the points in $T$, and therefore $T$ is bounded.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Finite T is bounded.

nodes.name: Conversely, a discrete set has an open cover by sets each holding one point
nodes.statement: Assume then that $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points of $T$. Since $T$ consists of isolated points, it has an open cover $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathrm{Pow}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that each set in $\mathcal{C}$ contains exactly one point $t\in T$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, a discrete set has an open cover by sets each holding one point.

nodes.name: Heine-Borel gives a finite subcover
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{C}$ is an open cover of $T$, and by the Heine-Borel theorem, there exists a finite subcover $\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of the set $T$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Heine-Borel gives a finite subcover.

nodes.name: Hence T is finite
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{D}$ is finite and each set in $\mathcal{D}$ contains exactly one point of $T$, the set $T$ must also be finite.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Hence T is finite.

nodes.name: Remains to express the three properties in first-order logic
nodes.statement: We then conclude the proof by establishing that there exists a first-order formula $\varphi(P)$ stating that the unary predicate $P$ is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Remains to express the three properties in first-order logic.

nodes.name: Define parallel(x,y,t,k)
nodes.statement:
We will first define a formula $\mathit{parallel}(x,y,t,k)$ stating that the lines defined by $x,y$ and $t,k$ are parallel in $(\mathbb{R}^n, eta)$. We define  egin{align*} &\mathit{parallel}(x,y,t,k):= x
eq y\wedge t
eq k \wedge \Big((\mathit{collinear}(x,y,t)\wedge \mathit{collinear}(x,y,k))\ &\quad\vee  ig(
eg\exists z(\mathit{collinear}(x,y,z)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(t,k,z))\ &\quad\quad\wedge \exists z_1 z_2(x
eq z_1\wedge\mathit{collinear}(x,y,z_1)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(x,t,z_2)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(z_1,z_2,k))\,  ig)\Big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Define parallel(x,y,t,k).

nodes.name: Plan simultaneous recursion for basis_k and flat_k
nodes.statement: We will then define first-order $\{\beta\}$-formulae $\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)$ and $\mathit{flat}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z)$ using simultaneous recursion. The first formula states that the vectors corresponding to the pairs $(x_0,x_i)$, $1\leq i\leq k$, form a basis of a $k$-dimensional flat. The second formula states that the point $z$ is in the span of the basis defined by the vectors $(x_0,x_i)$, the origin being $x_0$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Plan simultaneous recursion for basis_k and flat_k.

nodes.name: Recursive definitions of basis_k and flat_k
nodes.statement: First define $\mathit{basis}_0(x_0):= x_0=x_0$ and $\mathit{flat}_0(x_0,z):= x_0=z$. Then define $\mathit{flat}_k$ and $\mathit{basis_k}$ recursively in the following way. \begin{align*} &\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k):=\mathit{basis}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1})\wedge \neg \mathit{flat}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},x_k),\\ &\mathit{flat}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z):=\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)\\ &\quad\wedge \exists y_0\dots \exists y_k\Big(y_0=x_0 \wedge y_k=z \wedge\bigwedge_{i\, \leq\, k-1} \big(y_i=y_{i+1}\vee\mathit{parallel}(x_0,x_{i+1},y_i,y_{i+1})\big)\Big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Recursive definitions of basis_k and flat_k.

nodes.name: Idea of sepr(x,P): an n-dimensional triangle around x free of P
nodes.statement: We then define a first-order $\{\beta,P\}$-formula $\mathit{sepr}(x,P)$ asserting that $x$ belongs to an open ball $B$ such that each point in $B\setminus\{x\}$ belongs to the complement of $P$. The idea is to state that there exist $n+1$ points $x_0,\dots,x_n$ that form an \emph{$n$-dimensional triangle} around $x$, and every point contained in the triangle (with $x$ being a possible exception) belongs to the complement of $P$. Every open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is contained in some $n$-dimensional triangle in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and vice versa.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Idea of sepr(x,P): an n-dimensional triangle around x free of P.

nodes.name: Recursive definition of opentriangle_k
nodes.statement: will recursively define first-order formulae $\mathit{opentriangle}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z)$ stating that $z$ is properly inside a $k$-dimensional triangle defined by $x_0,\dots,x_k$, see Figure \ref{fig:opentriangle}. First define $\mathit{opentriangle}_1(x_0,x_1,z):=\beta^*(x_0,z,x_1)$, and then define \begin{align*} &\mathit{opentriangle}_{k}(x_0,\dots,x_k,z):=\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)\\ &\quad\wedge \exists y\big(\mathit{opentriangle}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},y)\wedge \beta^*(y,z,x_k)\big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Recursive definition of opentriangle_k.

nodes.name: Define sepr(x,P)
nodes.statement: We are now ready to define $\mathit{sepr}(x,P)$. Let \begin{multline*} \mathit{sepr}(x,P) := \exists x_0\dots \exists x_n\Bigl(\mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots, x_n,x)\\ \wedge \forall y \big((\mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n,y)\wedge y\neq x)\rightarrow \neg Py\big)\Bigr). \end{multline*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Define sepr(x,P).

nodes.name: phi_1 expresses closedness and phi_2 discreteness
nodes.statement: Now, the sentence $\varphi_1:=\forall x\bigl(\neg Px\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{sepr}(x,P)\bigr)$ states that each point in the complement of $P$ is contained in an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P$. The sentence therefore states that the complement of $P$ is a union of open balls. Since the set of unions of open balls is exactly the same as the set of open sets, the sentence states that $P$ is closed. The sentence $\varphi_2:=\forall x\bigl(Px\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{sepr}(x,P)\bigr)$ clearly states that $P$ consists of isolated points.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: phi_1 expresses closedness and phi_2 discreteness.

nodes.name: phi_3 expresses boundedness
nodes.statement: Finally, in order to state that $P$ is bounded, we define a formula asserting that there exist points $x_0,\dots,x_n$ that form an n-dimensional triangle around $P$. \begin{multline*} \varphi_3:=\exists x_0\dots \exists x_n\Bigl(\mathit{basis}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n) \wedge \forall y\bigl(Py\rightarrow \mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n,y)\bigr)\Bigr) \end{multline*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: phi_3 expresses boundedness.

nodes.name: The conjunction expresses finiteness
nodes.statement: The conjunction $\varphi_1\wedge\varphi_2\wedge\varphi_3$ states that $P$ is finite.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: The conjunction expresses finiteness.

nodes.name: Define sequence(P)
nodes.statement: Define \[ \mathit{sequence}(P):=\exists x\, Px\, \wedge\, \forall x\forall y\forall z\, \bigl(Px\wedge Py \wedge Pz\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{collinear}(x,y,z)\bigr). \] The formula $sequence(P)$ states that $P$ is a sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Define sequence(P).

nodes.name: Discrete spacing is first-order
nodes.statement: By inspection of Definition \ref{discretelyspaceddfn}, it is easy to see that there is a first-order formula $\psi$ such that the conjunction $sequence(P)\wedge\psi$ states that $P$ is a discretely spaced sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Discrete spacing is first-order.

nodes.name: The remaining definitions are first-order too
nodes.statement: Continuing this trend, it is straightforward to observe that Definitions \ref{discretelyinfinitedfn}, \ref{sequencewithzero} and \ref{omegalikedfn} specify first-order properties, and therefore there exists a first-order formula $\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ stating that $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: The remaining definitions are first-order too.

nodes.name: The zero-point is the base point; iterate unique successors to get (a_i)
nodes.statement: We denote by $i_0$ the unique zero-point of $P$. Since $P$ is a discretely infinite sequence, it has a base point. Clearly $i_0$ has to be the only base point of $P$. It is straightforward to establish that since $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence with the base point $i_0$, there exists a sequence $(a_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ of points $a_i\in P$ such that $i_0=a_0$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the unique $E$-successor of $a_{i}$ for all $i\in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: The zero-point is the base point; iterate unique successors to get (a_i).

nodes.name: h(i)=a_i is an embedding
nodes.statement: Define the function $h:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow P$ such that $h(i) = a_i$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $h$ is an embedding of $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: h(i)=a_i is an embedding.

nodes.name: For T = R^n show h is onto
nodes.statement: Assume then that $T=\mathbb{R}^n$. We shall show that the function $h:\mathbb{N}\longrightarrow P$ is a surjection.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: For T = R^n show h is onto.

nodes.name: Coordinatise the line containing P
nodes.statement: Let $d$ denote the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}$, and let $d_R$ be the restriction of the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to the line $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $P\subseteq R$. Let $g:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow R$ be the isometry from $(\mathbb{R},d)$ to $(R,d_R)$ such that $g(0) = i_0 = h(0)$ and such that for all $r\in\mathit{ran}(h)$, we have $\beta\bigl(i_0,g(1),r\bigr)$ or $\beta\bigl(i_0,r,g(1)\bigr)$. Let $(R,\leq^R)$ be the structure, where $$\leq^{R}\ =\ \{\ (u,v)\in R\times R\ |\ g^{-1}(u)\, \leq^{\mathbb{R}}\, g^{-1}(v)\ \}.$$
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Coordinatise the line containing P.

nodes.name: Reduce to ran(h) bounded above
nodes.statement: If $\mathit{ran}(h)$ is not bounded from above w.r.t. $\leq^R$, then $h$ must be a surjection. Therefore assume that $\mathit{ran}(h)$ is bounded above.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to ran(h) bounded above.

nodes.name: Take the least upper bound s, not in ran(h)
nodes.statement: By the Dedekind completeness of the reals, there exists a least upper bound $s\in R$ of $\mathit{ran}(h)$ w.r.t. $\leq^R$. Notice that since $h$ is an embedding of $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$, we have $s\not\in\mathit{ran}(h)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Take the least upper bound s, not in ran(h).

nodes.name: Suffices to show no point of P lies at or beyond s
nodes.statement: Due to the definition of $E$, it is sufficient to show that $\{\, t\in P\ |\ s\leq^R t\ \} = \emptyset$ in order to conclude that $h$ maps onto $P$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show no point of P lies at or beyond s.

nodes.name: s in P contradicts discrete spacing
nodes.statement: Assume that the least upper bound $s$ belongs to the set $P$. Since $P$ is a discretely spaced sequence, there is a point $u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{s\}$ such that $\beta(s,u,i_0)$ and $$\forall r\in\mathbb{R}^n \bigl(\beta^*(s,r,u) \rightarrow r\not\in P\bigl).$$ Now $u<^R s$ and the points $u$ and $s$ are linearly $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P)$-connected, implying that $s$ cannot be the least upper bound of $\mathit{ran}(h)$. This is a contradiction. Therefore $s\not\in P$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: s in P contradicts discrete spacing.

nodes.name: A point of P beyond s contradicts omega-likeness
nodes.statement: Assume, ad absurdum, that there exists a point $t\in P$ such that $\beta(i_0,s,t)$. Now, since $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence, there exists points $u',v'\in P\setminus\{s\}$ such that $\beta(u',s,v')$ and $$\forall r\in \mathbb{R}^n\bigl(\beta^*(u',r,v')\rightarrow r\not\in P\bigr).$$ We have $\beta(s,u',i_0)$ or $\beta(s,v',i_0)$. Assume, by symmetry, that $\beta(s,u',i_0)$. Now $u'<^R s$, and the points $u'$ and $s$ are linearly $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P)$-connected. Hence, since $s\not\in \mathit{ran}(h)$, we conclude that $s$ is not the least upper bound of $\mathit{ran}(h)$. This is a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: A point of P beyond s contradicts omega-likeness.

nodes.name: Fix S and an S-labelled Cartesian frame; aim to interpret a supergrid
nodes.statement: Let $S\not=\emptyset$ be a finite set of tile symbols. Let $\mathfrak{C} = (T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame. We shall show how an $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{G}_{\mathfrak{C}}$ is interpreted in $\mathfrak{C}$. Figures \ref{fig:triangle} and \ref{fig:triangle_tiled} illustrate the related constructions.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Fix S and an S-labelled Cartesian frame; aim to interpret a supergrid.

nodes.name: First family of lines through p_y
nodes.statement: The domain of the interpretation of $\mathfrak{G}_{\mathfrak{C}}$ in $\mathfrak{C}$ will be the set of intersection points of two sets of lines defined as follows. The first set of lines is formed by connecting the point $p_y$ to each of the points $u$ in the set $$\{x\in P\mid \beta(p_0,x,p_x)\}\setminus\{p_x\},$$ i.e., each line in the set corresponds to a pair $(u,p_y)$ for some $u\not=p_x$ such that $\beta(p_0,u,p_x)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: First family of lines through p_y.

nodes.name: Second family of lines through p_x
nodes.statement: Similarly, the second set of lines is formed by connecting the point $p_x$ to each of the points in the set $$\{x\in P\mid \beta(p_0,x,p_y)\}\setminus\{p_y\}.$$
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Second family of lines through p_x.

nodes.name: Define phi_Dom, phi_H, phi_V
nodes.statement:
We then define the formulae  egin{align*} \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\ := &\ \exists x y ig(P(x)\wedge P(y)\wedge eta^*(p_0,x,p_x)\wedge eta^*(p_0,y,p_y)\wedge eta^*(x,u,p_y)\wedge eta^*(y,u,p_x) ig)\ &\vee \Bigl(u
eq p_x\wedge u
eq p_y\wedge P(u)\wedge  igl( eta(p_0,u,p_x)\vee eta(p_0,u,p_y) igr) \Bigr),\ \varphi_{H}(u,v)\ :=&\ \exists x  igl( eta(p_0,x,p_y)\, \wedge\,  eta(x,u,v)\, \wedge\,  eta^*(u,v,p_x) igr) \wedge\,  orall r igl(\,  eta^*(u,r,v)\, ightarrow\, 
eg \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(r)\,  igr),\ \varphi_{V}(u,v)\ :=&\ \exists x  igl( eta(p_0,x,p_x)\, \wedge\,  eta(x,u,v)\, \wedge\,  eta^*(u,v,p_y) igr) \wedge\,  orall r igl(\,  eta^*(u,r,v)\, ightarrow\, 
eg \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(r)\,  igr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define phi_Dom, phi_H, phi_V.

nodes.name: Define diagonal(u,v)
nodes.statement: Next we define the following auxiliary formula: \begin{align*} \mathit{diagonal}(u,v):=& \exists x\bigl( \varphi_\mathit{Dom}(x)\wedge \varphi_\mathit{H}(u,x)\wedge\varphi_\mathit{V}(x,v)\bigr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define diagonal(u,v).

nodes.name: Recall N
nodes.statement: Recall the function $N$ that associates each tile type $t$ with the unique positive integer $N(t)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Recall N.

nodes.name: Define tile formulas by counting P-points on diagonals
nodes.statement: Let $\exists^{=N(t)}x$ denote the quantifier stating that there exist exactly $N(t)$ $x$:s. Now, for each tile symbol $P_t$, we define \begin{align*} \varphi_{P_t}(u)\ :=&\ \exists z \exists^{=N(t)} x \bigl(\, \varphi_\mathit{Dom}(z)\wedge\mathit{diagonal}(u,z) \wedge P(x)\wedge \beta^*(u,x,z)\, \bigr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define tile formulas by counting P-points on diagonals.

nodes.name: These formulas give I
nodes.statement: The formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_\mathit{H}$, $\varphi_\mathit{V}$ and $\varphi_{P(t)}$ define the uniform interpretation $I$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: These formulas give I.

nodes.name: Define the interpreted structure D_C
nodes.statement: Call $D_\mathfrak{C} := \{\ u\in T\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\ \}$, and define the structure $$\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C} = (D_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}},(P_t^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S}),$$ where \begin{align*} H^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}}\ :=&\ \{\ (u,v)\in D_\mathfrak{C}\times D_\mathfrak{C}\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_H(u,v)\ \}, \\ V^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}}\ :=&\ \{\ (u,v)\in D_\mathfrak{C}\times D_\mathfrak{C}\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_V(u,v)\ \},\\ P_t^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}}\ :=&\ \{\ u\in D_\mathfrak{C}\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_{P_t}(u)\ \}\text{ for each }P_t\in S. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define the interpreted structure D_C.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.7 embeds an S-labelled grid into D_C
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{nonstandardmodelsexcluded}, it is easy to see that there is and $S$-labelled grid $(G,H,V,(P_t)_{P_t\in S})$ such that there exists an injection $f$ from the domain of the grid to $D_{\mathfrak{C}}$ such that the following three conditions hold for all $u,v\in G$ and $P_t\in S$: \begin{enumerate} \item $(u,v)\in H\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{H}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $(u,v)\in V\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{V}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $u\in P_{t}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{P_t}\bigl( f(u)\bigr)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.7 embeds an S-labelled grid into D_C.

nodes.name: Hence D_C is isomorphic to an S-labelled supergrid
nodes.statement: Hence there is an $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}=(G_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}},(P_t^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S})$ such that there exists a bijection $f$ from $G_\mathfrak{C}$ to $D_\mathfrak{C}$ such that the following conditions hold for all $u,v\in G_{\mathfrak{C}}$ and $P_t\in S$: \begin{enumerate} \item $(u,v)\in H^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{H}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $(u,v)\in V^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{V}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $u\in P^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}}_{t}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{P_t}\bigl( f(u)\bigr)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Hence D_C is isomorphic to an S-labelled supergrid.

nodes.name: Define G(T,S)
nodes.statement: Let $$\mathcal{G}(T,S):=\{\ \mathfrak{G}_{\mathfrak{C}}\in\mathcal{G}_S \ |\ \mathfrak{C}\in\mathcal{C}(T,S)\ \}.$$
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define G(T,S).

nodes.name: G(T,S) contains all S-labelled grids and I interprets it
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $\mathfrak{G}_S\subseteq\mathcal{G}(T,S)$. The function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{G}(T,S)$ in $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: G(T,S) contains all S-labelled grids and I interprets it.

nodes.name: Fix vocabularies sigma and tau
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma = \{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of supergrids, and let $\tau = \{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled Cartesian frames.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Fix vocabularies sigma and tau.

nodes.name: Frame-defining sentence from Lemma 4.12
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{boxedcartesianpicturesdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$ denote such a sentence.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Frame-defining sentence from Lemma 4.12.

nodes.name: Tiling sentence from Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_{S}$ such that a structure $\mathfrak{A}$ of the vocabulary $\sigma$ is $S$-tilable if and only if there is an expansion $\mathfrak{A}^*$ of the structure $\mathfrak{A}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{A}^*\models\varphi_{S}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Tiling sentence from Lemma 2.5.

nodes.name: Interpretation I from Lemma 4.13
nodes.statement: Now recall Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}. By Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}, since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, there exists a computable function $I$ such that for each input $S$ to the tiling problem, the function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of some class $\mathcal{G}(T,S)\supseteq \mathfrak{G}_S$ of $S$-labelled supergrids in the class $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$ of all $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Interpretation I from Lemma 4.13.

nodes.name: Define psi_S
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an input to the tiling problem. Define the $\tau$-sentence \[ \psi_{S}\, :=\, \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S\, \wedge\, I(\, \varphi_{S}\, ). \]
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define psi_S.

nodes.name: Goal: psi_S satisfiable iff the grid is S-tilable
nodes.statement: We will prove that for each input $S$ to the tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There \emph{exists} an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$. \item The grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Goal: psi_S satisfiable iff the grid is S-tilable.

nodes.name: psi_S satisfiable in an expansion
nodes.statement: There \emph{exists} an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: psi_S satisfiable in an expansion.

nodes.name: The grid is S-tilable
nodes.statement: The grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: The grid is S-tilable.

nodes.name: This gives a reduction from the complement of the tiling problem
nodes.statement: Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the \emph{complement problem} of the tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: This gives a reduction from the complement of the tiling problem.

nodes.name: The complement of a Pi^0_1-complete problem is Sigma^0_1-complete
nodes.statement: Since the tiling problem is $\Pi_1^0$-complete, its complement problem is $\Sigma_1^0$-complete.\footnote{It is of course a well-known triviality that the complement $\overline{A}$ of a problem $A$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-hard if $A$ is $\Pi^0_1$-hard. Choose an arbitrary problem $B\in \Sigma^0_1$. Therefore $\overline{B}\in\Pi^0_1$. By the hardness of $A$, there is a computable reduction $f$ such that $x\in\overline{B}\Leftrightarrow f(x)\in A$, whence $x\in B\Leftrightarrow f(x)\in \overline{A}$.}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: The complement of a Pi^0_1-complete problem is Sigma^0_1-complete.

nodes.name: Tilable grid gives a frame satisfying psi_S (Lemma 2.1)
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an input to the tiling problem. Assume first that the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{G}^*$ of the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ to the vocabulary $\{H,V\}\, \cup\, S$ such that $\mathfrak{G}^*\models\varphi_{S}$. Now since $\mathfrak{G}^*\in\mathfrak{G}_S\subseteq\mathcal{G}(T,S)$, by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} there exists an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models I(\varphi_{S})$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame, we have $\mathfrak{C}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S\wedge I(\varphi_{S})$. Hence the Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\psi_S$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Tilable grid gives a frame satisfying psi_S (Lemma 2.1).

nodes.name: A model of psi_S gives a tilable supergrid, hence a tilable grid
nodes.statement: For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that we have $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models I(\varphi_{S})$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame with the domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models I(\varphi_{S})$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_{S}$ for some $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{G}(T,S)$. Thus there exists a supergrid that is $S$-tilable. Hence the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: A model of psi_S gives a tilable supergrid, hence a tilable grid.

nodes.name: Same as the proof of Theorem 4.15
nodes.statement: The proof is essentially the same as the proof of Theorem \ref{infinitelemma}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Same as the proof of Theorem 4.15.

nodes.name: Use Lemma 4.14 and reduce from recurrent tiling
nodes.statement: The main difference is that we use Lemma \ref{recurrencegridinterpr} and interpret a class of labelled recurrence grids instead of a class of labelled supergrids, and hence obtain a reduction from the recurrent tiling problem instead of the ordinary tiling problem.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma 4.14 and reduce from recurrent tiling.

nodes.name: Gives Pi^1_1-hardness
nodes.statement: Thereby we establish $\Pi^1_1$-hardness instead of $\Sigma_1^0$-hardness.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Gives Pi^1_1-hardness.

nodes.name: The isomorphism part of Lemma 4.7 is essential
nodes.statement: Due to the recurrence condition of the recurrent tiling problem, the result of Lemma \ref{nonstandardmodelsexcluded} that there is an isomorphism from $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ to $(P,E)$---rather than an embedding---is essential.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: The isomorphism part of Lemma 4.7 is essential.

nodes.name: Fix an S-labelled m x k Cartesian frame; aim to interpret an m x k torus
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ Cartesian frame. We shall show how to interpret an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ torus $\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}$ in $\mathfrak{C}$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Fix an S-labelled m x k Cartesian frame; aim to interpret an m x k torus.

nodes.name: Similar to Lemma 4.13
nodes.statement: The idea behind the interpretation is quite similar to the idea behind the interpretation in the proof of Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Similar to Lemma 4.13.

nodes.name: Reuse the formulas of Lemma 4.13
nodes.statement: Recall the formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_{H}$, $\varphi_{V}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}$ defined in the proof of Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}. We shall now define variants of these formulae suitable for interpreting $S$-labelled tori in $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames. In the definitions of the new formulae, we shall make use of the old formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_{H}$, $\varphi_{V}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Reuse the formulas of Lemma 4.13.

nodes.name: Define the wrap-around variants of the formulas
nodes.statement: We define \begin{align*} \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)&\ :=\ \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\wedge \exists x\exists y\bigl(\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(x)\wedge \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(y)\wedge \varphi_H(u,x)\wedge \varphi_V(u,y) \bigr),\\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(u,v)&\ :=\ \varphi_H(u,v) \vee\Big(\beta(p_0,v,p_y)\wedge\beta(v,u,p_x)\wedge \forall x\big(\beta^*(u,x,p_x)\rightarrow\neg\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^{\mathit{fin}}(x)\big)\Big),\\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(u,v)&\ :=\ \varphi_V(u,v) \vee\Big(\beta(p_0,v,p_x)\wedge\beta(v,u,p_y)\wedge \forall x\big(\beta^*(u,x,p_y)\rightarrow\neg\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^{\mathit{fin}}(x)\big)\Big),\\ \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(u)&\ :=\ \varphi_{P_t}(u)\text{ for each }P_t\in S. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Define the wrap-around variants of the formulas.

nodes.name: Define the interpreted structure F_C
nodes.statement: Let $F_\mathfrak{C}:=\{u\in T \mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_{Dom}(u)\}$. Define the structure $$\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}=\bigl(F_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}, (P_t^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S}\bigr),$$ where \begin{align*} H^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{(u,v)\in F_\mathfrak{C}\times F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(u,v)\}, \\ V^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{(u,v)\in F_\mathfrak{C}\times F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(u,v)\}, \\ P_t^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{u\in F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(u)\}, \end{align*} for all $P_t\in S$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Define the interpreted structure F_C.

nodes.name: F_C is isomorphic to an S-labelled m x k torus
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to check that there exists an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ torus \[ \mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{C}}=\bigl(D,H^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}, (P_t^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S}\bigr) \] and a bijection $f$ from $D$ to $F_\mathfrak{C}$ such that the following conditions hold for all $u,v\in D$. \begin{enumerate} \item $(u,v)\in H^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(f(u),f(v))$, \vspace{1pt} \item $(u,v)\in V^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(f(u),f(v))$, \vspace{1pt} \item $u\in P_t^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(f(u))$ for all $P_t\in S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: F_C is isomorphic to an S-labelled m x k torus.

nodes.name: Frames of all sizes and labellings exist since T extends linearly in 2D
nodes.statement: Notice that since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, there exist $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames of all sizes $m\times k$ with all possible $S$-labelling configurations in the class $\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{fin}}(T,S)$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Frames of all sizes and labellings exist since T extends linearly in 2D.

nodes.name: The formulas define J
nodes.statement: We have hence established that for all finite sets $S\not=\emptyset$ of tile symbols, the class of $S$-labelled tori is uniformly first-order interpretable in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$. Furthermore, the formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^\mathit{fin}$, $\varphi_H^\mathit{fin}$, $\varphi_V^\mathit{fin}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}^\mathit{fin}$ define the desired uniform interpretation $J$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: The formulas define J.

nodes.name: Fix vocabularies sigma and tau
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma=\{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of tori, and let $\tau=\{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled finite Cartesian frames.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Fix vocabularies sigma and tau.

nodes.name: Finite-frame sentence from Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{finitedefinable}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi^S_{\mathit{fCf}}$ denote such a sentence.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Finite-frame sentence from Lemma 5.5.

nodes.name: Interpretation J from Lemma 5.6
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{torusinterpretablelemma}, there is a computable function $J$ such that for all inputs $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with domain $T$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Interpretation J from Lemma 5.6.

nodes.name: Tiling sentence from Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_S$ such that for all tori $\mathfrak{B}$, the torus $\mathfrak{B}$ is $S$-tilable iff there is an expansion $\mathfrak{B}^*$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^*\models\varphi_{S}$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Tiling sentence from Lemma 2.5.

nodes.name: Define gamma_S
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. Define the first-order $\tau$-sentence \[ \gamma_S:=\varphi_{\mathit{fCf}}^S\wedge J(\varphi_S). \]
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Define gamma_S.

nodes.name: Goal: gamma_S satisfiable iff some torus is S-tilable
nodes.statement: We will prove that for each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. \item There exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Goal: gamma_S satisfiable iff some torus is S-tilable.

nodes.name: gamma_S satisfiable with finite P
nodes.statement: There exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: gamma_S satisfiable with finite P.

nodes.name: Some torus is S-tilable
nodes.statement: There exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Some torus is S-tilable.

nodes.name: This reduces the complement of periodic tiling
nodes.statement: Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the complement problem of the periodic tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ with a finite predicate.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: This reduces the complement of periodic tiling.

nodes.name: The complement is Pi^0_1-complete
nodes.statement: Since the periodic tiling problem is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete, its complement problem is $\Pi^0_1$-complete.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: The complement is Pi^0_1-complete.

nodes.name: A tilable torus yields a finite frame satisfying gamma_S
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an input to the periodic tiling problem. First assume that there exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{T}^*$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{T}^*\models \varphi_S$. Since the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$, and since $\mathfrak{T}^*\models\varphi_S$, it follows by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that there exists an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models J(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame, we have that $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}\wedge J(\varphi_S)$. Hence the finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\gamma_S$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: A tilable torus yields a finite frame satisfying gamma_S.

nodes.name: A model of gamma_S yields a tilable torus
nodes.statement: For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models J_S(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame with domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models J(\varphi_S)$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_S$ holds for some $S$-labelled torus $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma} there exists a torus that is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: A model of gamma_S yields a tilable torus.
